Background
The American Society of Naval Engineering (ASNE) holds an annual competition
surrounding the creation and innovation of electrically powered, remote controlled boats from
teams around the country. With ever increasing electrical influence in the world, the opportunity
of technological advancement becomes increasingly feasible. Several design requirements have
to be met in order to qualify for competition. The competition involves driving the craft along a
2-mile long body of water with the considerations of function, speed, and effectiveness within
the design. This team inherited a design from years prior, and the goal was to provide an updated
extension of the internal electrical system.
The inherited vessel included a custom aluminum hull, one propeller, one water pump,
some batteries, a remote control, and an electric motor. New designs needed to revolve around
fixing old issues and adapting to new guidelines. Main issues included overheating of the motor
and power efficiency; therefore, the outdated electrical hardware needed to be replaced. Given
this year’s competition requires the boat to hold an extra 60 pounds of weight throughout
demonstration, something must have been introduced for the purpose of extra buoyancy. Other
notable mandatory parameters are: not exceeding 55 volts as an input to the electrical system,
teams are allowed a 5-minute setup on competition day, and the time frame to perform within
cannot exceed 55 minutes.
​

fixing old issues and adapting to new guidelines. Main issues included overheating of the motor
and power efficiency; therefore, the outdated electrical hardware needed to be replaced. Given

Electrical Design and Analysis
One of the major sources of improvement we decided to tackle this year was the improvement
of the electrical/cooling system. The previous team from 2024 reported multiple instances of
overheating, leading their control system to stop working ⅖ miles into their race and not
completing the competition. ​
​
The original control system used 6, 22.2V LIPO batteries in parallel with a 3300mAh capacity
each. Giving them a total capacity of 19.2 Ah. The parallel connections were done with multiple
EC5 connector y splitters, having a total of 7 y splitters to connect all of the batteries to the one
connector on the ECS. The Flycolor 150a ECS was then connected to a KingVal 4092 800KV
motor for the power delivery to the water. As well as the Flysky FS-iA6 remote control receiver
controlling the motor speed and servo turning.​
​
Once we had fully analysed how this old control system worked, we decided on multiple
different design changes to improve the function and safety of this system. First was the upsizing
of the battery pack to 8 in parallel, giving us 6600mah more than the last design giving our motor
more range to run. We saw that the previous team had done 2 of their 5 miles, and although the
rules state we only need to go 2 miles now. We decided adding more of a safety margin was a no
brainer. ​
​
The second electrical change was the overhauling of the wiring system, removing all of the y
splitters and replacing them with parallel bus bars. All of the positive battery connections are
connected to one bus bar, with the negative side being connected to another. This gives us
cleaner wiring, and less points of failure if one y splitter failed or burnt out in the previous
design.
A third major change is introducing a 150a circuit breaker on the positive busbar feed, as in the
previous design there was no power shutoff. There was only a pwm switch to disable the steering
receiver, but introducing a proper power cutoff and overcurrent protection was ideal for us to
introduce. The system was always live, leading to popping and sparking when disconnecting or
connecting batteries. With the new system we can now disable the switch on the breaker, connect
all the batteries. And then connect the switch to connect the load at once, instead of having to
connect it unbalanced.

Our final major electrical change was to tackle the problem of the pump, the previous team
reported multiple overheating issues with it. When we analyzed the flow out of our pump we
first noticed that it had an advertised flow rate of 1.8 L/min, but we could only measure about
half that much out of it. Upon diagnosing we realized that this pump would always run when the
system had power, it had only a 2 pin connector. Meaning that the 3 pin pwm signal from the
receiver had no way to tell it when to run. We decided introducing a pwm controlled switch was
ideal for this, as now the signal from the receiver can toggle the switch which can turn our pump
off. Allowing us to never dry run it and ruin the pump again, and replacing the pump got our
flow back to the advertised rate we should have for our cooling system.

Electrical Design Progress
​
The electrical system design proposed for this year’s vessel has been fully implemented,
and it’s a big step forward in terms of reliability and overall performance. All of the planned
upgrades, including the larger battery system, new wiring layout, and added circuit protection,
have been completed. Because of delays with the hull redesign, we haven’t been able to fully test
the system in the water yet. That said, all of the electrical components have been tested out of the
water and are working as expected.
The battery system was upgraded from six to eight 22.2V LiPo batteries in parallel, which
increases the total capacity and gives us a much better safety margin for runtime. This was an
easy decision, since the previous team wasn’t able to complete the race distance. Even though the
requirement is now only 2 miles, we wanted to make sure we had more than enough capacity to
avoid running into the same issue.
We also completely redesigned the wiring system. The old setup used a lot of EC5
Y-splitters, which made things cluttered and introduced multiple points of failure. In the new
design, all connections are routed through positive and negative bus bars. This makes the system
much cleaner, easier to work on, and reduces the chances of something overheating or failing at a
connection point.
Another major improvement was adding a 150A circuit breaker to the positive bus bar.
The previous system didn’t have a real power cutoff and was always live, which led to sparking
when connecting batteries. Now, we can safely connect everything first and then turn the system
on using the breaker. This makes the system a lot safer and easier to handle.
Overall, while we haven’t been able to fully test everything in the water yet, we’re in a
much better position than the previous design. We hope that these improvements will solve the
issues seen last year and allow the system to run more reliably once it’s fully integrated with the
hull and tested under real conditions.

Determining Buoyant Force from the Outriggers
​

To offset the mandated payload of 60 lbs and assist the boat in rising during acceleration,

we analyzed the buoyancy provided by two cylindrical PVC outriggers mounted along the sides
of the hull. According to Archimedes’ principle, the upward buoyant force on an object is equal
to the weight of the water it displaces:

Hydrodynamic role of Outriggers in Planing
​
The outriggers contribute to the vessel’s performance not only through buoyancy, but also
through their effect on the boat’s trim and dynamic behavior. After accounting for their own
weight, the outriggers provide a net upward force of 74.74 lbs, which exceeds the 60 lb payload
and results in a 14.74 lb reduction in the effective load acting on the hull.
For the vessel to achieve and sustain planing, the total upward force must be greater than the
effective weight:
𝐹𝑙𝑖𝑓𝑡 > 𝑊𝑒𝑓𝑓𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑣𝑒
The upward force consists of both static lift and dynamic life. Static lift is provided by buoyancy
from displaced water, and dynamic lift is generated as the hull moves through the water. The
downward forces on the system include the total system weight, meaning the payload and the
onboard components. By providing net buoyancy greater than the weight of the system, the
outriggers reduce the ‘effective weight’ that must be supported hydrodynamically. Additionally,
the outriggers are positioned along the sides of the hull and angled slightly upward, this shifts the
center of buoyancy rearward and promotes an increase in bow pitch angle. As a result, the front
of the hull will have an easier time rising out of the water during acceleration. This combination

Hull Design Progress
The hull design for this year’s vessel has been mostly finalized, and all of the necessary
components for the outrigger system have been obtained. This design focuses on improving both
stability and buoyancy to better support the increased payload. The addition of 8-inch PVC
outriggers is a key part of this approach, as they are expected to provide significant additional
buoyant force and help maintain a more stable platform in the water.
At this point, all materials are ready, but the final assembly of the outriggers is still in progress.
The main challenge has been the welding required to securely attach the outrigger supports to the
hull. Since no one on the team has prior welding experience, we reached out to the UGA
machine shop for assistance. While they have been helpful, there have been some delays in
coordinating support, which has slowed down the overall progress of the hull assembly. We have
assembled the caps on two of the PVC pipes, but we are waiting on the weather to get warmer to
fill them with marine foam. The listing says the ambient temperature must be at least 73 degrees,
and here in Athens it will be in the low 80’s at the end of this week, which is when we are
planning to finish assembling the outriggers.
Once the welding is completed and the outriggers are fully integrated, the hull will be ready for
full system integration and in-water testing. We are currently waiting on this final step and are
hopeful that we will be able to move forward soon. With the hull completed, we’ll finally be able
to test how the buoyancy, stability, and electrical systems all work together under real operating
conditions.

Risks
One major risk with adding a 60 lb payload is the overall increase in system weight.
While it likely won’t cause the boat to sink, it will make the hull sit deeper in the water, which
increases the wetted surface area and therefore drag. This also reduces freeboard, so the boat is
more vulnerable to taking on water from waves or wake. On top of that, if the weight isn’t
distributed well, it can negatively affect stability by raising the center of gravity. To help offset
this, the design uses 8-inch PVC outriggers that provide about 74.74 lbs of buoyant force, which
helps support the added load and improves stability. Beyond that, keeping heavier components
low and centered and using lightweight materials where possible will help manage the added
weight more effectively.
Another concern is the increase in drag caused by the heavier system. As the boat sits
lower in the water, more of the hull is exposed to fluid resistance, which makes it harder for the
propulsion system to maintain speed. This added load can also put more strain on the motor and
contribute to overheating, which has already been an issue in past designs. To address this, the
hull and outrigger setup should be as streamlined as possible, with everything aligned in the
direction of motion and minimal unnecessary surface area exposed to the water. Smoothing
surfaces and keeping components or wiring out of the water can also help reduce drag. In
addition, using a motor and propeller setup that is better suited for higher loads can help
compensate for the increased resistance, but this may require further electronic redesign.
A final challenge is the limited space available inside the hull for all the required
components. As more systems are added, the layout can become crowded, making it harder to
maintain, increasing the risk of poor weight distribution, and limiting airflow for cooling. This
can lead to overheating and reduced reliability. To improve this, components can be arranged in
layers, with heavier items like batteries placed at the bottom, control electronics above them, and
lighter components on top. Using modular mounts can make it easier to access and adjust
components as needed. If space is still an issue, some components can be moved to sealed
external enclosures, as long as they are properly waterproofed. Adding ventilation or cooling
solutions can also help manage heat and improve overall system performance.
